---
title: "Pooling"
description: "A neural-network operation that summarizes nearby values, commonly reducing the spatial size of feature maps."
term: "Pooling"
letter: "P"
category: "Computer Vision"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

Pooling summarizes a small neighborhood of values. In an image model, it can
shrink a feature map while keeping a coarse signal about what was detected.
Max pooling keeps the largest value in each neighborhood; average pooling
keeps the mean.

## Technical explanation

A pooling layer applies a reduction over windows of an input tensor, with
choices such as window size, stride, padding, and reduction function. A
spatial pooling operation typically reduces height and width while leaving
the channel dimension unchanged.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Downsampling can reduce later computation and memory use and can make a
representation less sensitive to small shifts. It also discards detail, so
the operation must suit the task; dense localization tasks may need to
preserve spatial resolution.

## How it works

For each window, the layer computes a statistic such as its maximum or
average. With a 2-by-2 max-pooling window and stride 2, each non-overlapping
2-by-2 region becomes one value. During backpropagation, gradients are routed
through the values selected or averaged by the pooling operation.

## Practical example

A convolutional image classifier may apply a 2-by-2 max-pooling layer after
convolution and activation. This halves each spatial dimension when stride is
2, reducing the size of the feature maps passed to later layers.

## Common misconceptions

- Pooling is not the same as resizing an input image; it operates on
  intermediate feature tensors.
- Pooling does not always improve accuracy. Strided convolutions or
  architectures that preserve resolution may be preferable.
